The full translation already fits: it's about 183 words, under the 200 limit. Here it is again:

On the Moon there's no doctor nearby, and communication with Earth is delayed, so the crew has to spot a health problem early and decide on their own what to do. Lunar Health is a web app that brings the health of an entire lunar base crew into one place and explains it in plain language. A dashboard ranks astronauts by severity. Each reading appears first as a plain word (Normal, High, Very low), followed by its value, its range and its source. Every out-of-range parameter says what to do and who to escalate to: self-care, the crew or the flight surgeon. The app covers all three stages of the mission. Life on the base includes vital signs, cognitive and psychological tests, nutrition and lab work. The moonwalk covers live suit telemetry and radiation on a real map of the south pole. At the airlock, a check-out blocks egress when there's a critical risk, and a check-in schedules follow-ups at 2 and 24 hours. Measurements and tests are based on the NASA Standard Measures, the Human Research Program risks and the NASA-STD-3001 standard.
details:
What exactly does it do? Lunar Health supports each astronaut through all three stages of a surface mission and tells them in plain words how they're doing and what to do. On the base, it shows 13 daily parameters, including sleep, blood pressure, heart rate, blood oxygen, glucose, hydration, nutrition, mood, crew relations and stress. It also offers five tests (a daily check-in, the PVT cognitive vigilance test, the weekly PANAS questionnaire, the PSS-14 perceived stress scale and a balance test), plus a meal log and lab and imaging results. At the airlock, a guided check-out reviews the plan, symptoms, vital signs, cognitive test, balance and suit, and it blocks egress if any item is critical. During the moonwalk, it shows live suit pressure, heart rate, temperature, breathing, radiation and dose, suit consumables, time left to return and the route on a real map of the south pole. On return, the check-in records symptoms of decompression sickness and lunar dust irritation and schedules follow-ups at 2 h and 24 h.

How does it work? All data uses a single status scale: Normal (green), Caution (amber), Alert (red) and No data (gray), always shown with both color and text. Each parameter has its own thresholds, an explanation of why it matters on the Moon, what to do in each state and its scientific source, all configurable in one place. For example, the PVT counts a lapse above 355 ms (Basner et al., 2011), and radiation is compared against the lunar background of about 57 µSv/h measured by Chang'e 4. The dashboard shows one indicator per astronaut, each profile shows the details and each parameter shows its 14-day history. The questionnaires and the balance test can be voice-guided. The app runs in the browser and stores data on the device, so it keeps working even if the link to Earth drops. Suit telemetry is simulated for the demo.

What are the benefits? It gives the crew the autonomy to detect problems and act without waiting for Earth, and it tells them when they do need to escalate to the flight surgeon. It doesn't assume astronauts know how to interpret medical data. It keeps anyone from heading out with a critical risk and sets up follow-up after every EVA. Every number can be traced back to its source.

What do we hope to achieve? We want health monitoring to stop being a job for the doctor on Earth and become an everyday tool for the crew. The next steps are connecting real sensors (watches, pulse oximeters, the suit), validating the thresholds with an aerospace medicine team and testing the app in analog missions. The same approach works on Earth for Antarctic bases, offshore platforms and communities with no doctor nearby.

What tools, programming languages, hardware or software do we use? TypeScript, Next.js 16 (App Router) and React 19; Tailwind CSS 4 and shadcn/ui-style components built on Radix; Recharts for trend charts; Zustand for state and in-browser persistence; lucide-react for icons; and the browser's Web Speech API for reading aloud. The interface is available in Spanish and English. It needs no special hardware and runs in any modern browser on a computer or tablet. The architecture is a modular monolith (monitoring, telemetry, airlock, tests, nutrition and lab results), ready to connect real sensors or a backend without changing the interface.
